Joint Quantization and Dynamic Partitioning for
Context-Aware Edge Vision Transformers
Jiaqi Zhu
Walmart
Sunnyvale, USA
jiaqi.zhu@walmart.com
Prakriti Jain
Heidelberg University
Heidelberg, Germany
prakriti.jain@stud.uni-heidelberg.de
Dewant Katare
Technische Universiteit Delft
Delft, the Netherlands
d.katare@tudelft.nl
Saurabh Kumar
Walmart
Sunnyvale, USA
saurabh.kumar4@walmart.com
Abstract—Deploying vision transformer models across con-
nected and automated vehicles (CAVs) requires joint management
of computation and Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication.
Static split-inference methods use fixed partition points and
cannot adapt to time-varying link bandwidth, processing load,
and concurrent multi-stream traffic. This paper proposes an
edge orchestration framework that jointly selects model partition
points, per-layer quantization bitwidths, and execution placement
across heterogeneous vehicular compute nodes. The joint parti-
tioning and mixed-precision allocation problem is formulated as a
Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) that minimizes compute
and communication energy subject to end-to-end latency and
task-quality constraints. The framework is evaluated on Jetson
Orin Nano (8 GB), Jetson Orin NX (16 GB), and Jetson AGX
Orin (32 GB) nodes using OPV2V-driven multi-stream workloads
with K ∈{2, 4, 6, 8}. Across the evaluated configurations, the
proposed formulation reduces V2V communication energy by
33.3–36.0% relative to a Uniform INT8 split. At K = 8, end-to-
end task completion latency is reduced by 34.0% on the Orin
Nano and 33.1% on the Orin NX relative to the same baseline,
while limiting the reduction in 3D detection accuracy to 3.1–4.1
percentage points in mAP50 relative to FP16 execution.
Index Terms—Edge AI, Split Inference, Mixed-Precision Quan-
tization, Vehicular Edge Computing, Vision Transformers
I. INTRODUCTION
Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) process camera,
LiDAR, and other sensor streams to maintain situational
awareness under changing traffic conditions. Transformer-
based perception models provide strong performance for visual
and spatio-temporal tasks by modeling long-range depen-
dencies across input features [1], [2]. Their deployment on
embedded platforms, however, introduces high computation,
memory, and energy requirements [2], [3]. Distributed execu-
tion provides an alternative when local processing alone cannot
satisfy the required latency or resource limits. In this setting,
part of the inference graph executes on the sensing platform
and the remaining computation is transferred to a second
edge node [4], [5]. Split inference introduces a direct trade-
off between local computation and communication. Moving
the partition deeper into the model increases the computation
retained on the local node, while an earlier partition offloads
more execution but may require transmission of a larger
intermediate activation [4], [6]. This trade-off becomes more
difficult under concurrent vehicular inference because layer
execution time changes with processing load and the available
V2V data rate may differ across streams. A cut selected for
one compute or link condition can therefore increase either
completion latency or communication energy when these
conditions change.
Existing methods address individual parts of this problem.
Dynamic DNN partitioning and task offloading adapt execu-
tion to compute and network conditions [5], [7], while adaptive
semantic communication reduces the amount of intermediate
information transmitted during distributed inference [6], [8].
Quantization reduces arithmetic and memory cost by executing
network operations at lower numerical precision
[9]–[11].
Energy-aware CAV and edge–cloud frameworks have also
considered adaptive deployment and resource allocation [12],
[13]. These approaches do not jointly determine the stream-
specific partition location and layer-wise numerical precision
while accounting for their combined effect on compute energy,
intermediate activation size, and V2V transmission cost.
This paper presents an edge orchestration framework for
joint partition and mixed-precision selection in vehicular Vi-
sion Transformer inference. For each stream, the framework
selects a contiguous local-to-aggregator partition, while a
common layer-wise INT8/FP16 configuration is selected for
the deployed model. The resulting problem is formulated
as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) that minimizes
compute and V2V communication energy subject to per-
stream end-to-end latency and task-quality constraints. The
formulation uses profiled concurrency-dependent layer latency,
precision-dependent activation size, stream-specific V2V link
rate, and empirically calibrated quantization sensitivity.
The framework is evaluated on a heterogeneous NVIDIA
Jetson Orin testbed. Jetson Orin Nano (8 GB) and Jetson
Orin NX (16 GB) are evaluated as alternative local compute
nodes, with Jetson AGX Orin (32 GB) acting as the edge
aggregator. Experiments use OPV2V-driven workloads with
K ∈{2, 4, 6, 8} concurrent streams under emulated V2V link
conditions. System performance is measured using end-to-end
task completion latency, compute energy, V2V communication
energy, and 3D detection mAP50. The research contributions
are as follows:
• We formulate stream-specific model partitioning and
layer-wise INT8/FP16 selection as a MILP that mini-
mizes compute and V2V communication energy under
latency and task-quality constraints.
arXiv:2611.14196v1  [cs.AI]  10 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
• We couple precision-dependent execution cost and in-
termediate activation size with the partition decision,
allowing the optimizer to account for both local compute
load and stream-specific V2V transmission cost.
• We evaluate the formulation on three edge devices using
configurations K ∈{2, 4, 6, 8} concurrent OPV2V-driven
streams, reporting energy, task completion latency, solver
runtime, and 3D detection accuracy against static FP16
and uniform INT8 deployments.
This paper is organized as follows. Section II discusses split
inference, quantization, and communication-aware vehicular
edge execution. Section III presents the system model and
MILP formulation. Section IV describes the experimental
setup. Section V presents the evaluation results, and Section VI
concludes the paper.
II. RELATED WORK
Distributed inference of Vision Transformers across con-
nected vehicles requires balancing split inference bound-
aries, numerical compression, and multi-stream execution con-
straints. This section surveys recent developments in model
partitioning, communication-aware edge inference, and ve-
hicular edge computing, highlighting the methodological gap
addressed by our joint formulation.
A. Split Inference and Dynamic Partitioning
Split inference divides neural network between a resource-
constrained sensing platform and a more capable edge node.
Matsubara and Levorato [4] partition object-detection net-
works and transmit intermediate features between mobile and
edge platforms, showing that the selected cut affects both local
execution and communication cost. The benefit of a partition
therefore depends on the computational cost retained before
the cut and the size of the activation transferred afterward.
Recent work considers partition selection under changing edge
conditions. Zhang et al. [5] jointly address DNN partitioning
and task offloading using reinforcement learning under varying
compute and communication conditions and concurrent task
arrivals. Uslu and Dagdeviren [7] study optimization methods
for distributed DNN and large-model inference, including
partitioning, communication, and resource allocation. Katare et
al. [13] consider adaptive resource allocation across serverless
edge–cloud environments. These approaches support adaptive
execution or resource assignment, but numerical precision is
not jointly selected with the partition boundary.
B. Quantization and Communication-Aware Edge Inference
Quantization reduces model memory and arithmetic cost
by mapping weights and activations to lower numerical pre-
cision
[9], [11]. Moosmann et al.
[10] evaluate fully
quantized object-detection models on low-power embedded
systems, while Gaddi [9] studies post-training quantization
for a transformer-based autonomous driving network. These
methods address reduced-precision execution, but the selected
bitwidth is not coupled to the communication cost of an
intermediate split. Communication-oriented methods instead
TABLE I: Comparison of Representative Edge AI Approaches

CAV
modify the intermediate data transmitted between compute
nodes. Devoto et al. [6] adapt semantic token communication
for transformer-based edge inference according to network
conditions. Wang et al. [8] analyze communication overhead
together with inference latency and reliability, while Fu et
al. [3] discuss communication-efficient and task-oriented op-
timization for edge AI inference. These methods address the
transmission side of distributed inference, but do not jointly
select layer precision and the stream-specific partition point.
C. Vehicular Edge Execution
Vehicular inference have changing link conditions and con-
tinuous sensing to the partitioning problem. Mayumu et al.
[14] study multimodal information processing and exchange in
V2X systems. Katare et al. [12] consider model partitioning,
adaptive deployment, and approximation for energy-aware
CAV computing. These studies motivate adaptive compute
and communication decisions in vehicular systems, but do
not jointly optimize layer-wise precision and stream-specific
partitioning under a common compute and V2V energy ob-
jective [15]. Table I compares representative methods with
the formulation used in this paper. The comparison focuses
on whether partition selection, precision or communication
adaptation, and concurrent workload execution are consid-
ered together. Existing work provides mechanisms for dy-
namic partitioning, reduced-precision execution, or commu-
nication adaptation, but these decisions are generally ad-
dressed separately. The formulation in this paper couples
the stream-specific partition boundary with a common layer-
wise INT8/FP16 configuration, allowing precision-dependent
compute cost and transmitted activation size to enter the same
energy minimization problem.
III. SYSTEM MODEL AND OPTIMIZATION FORMULATION
This section formalizes the joint model partitioning, layer-
wise precision allocation, and execution placement framework.
We first outline the multi-tier vehicular execution pipeline
illustrated in Fig. 1, establish exact binary linearizations for the
coupled decision variables, and formulate the Mixed-Integer
Linear Program (MILP) that minimizes total energy consump-
tion under end-to-end latency and task-quality constraints.
A. System Architecture
We consider a two-node split-inference configuration se-
lected from a three-device vehicular edge testbed, depicted
in Fig. 1. The local on-vehicle node is either an NVIDIA
Jetson Orin Nano (8 GB), denoted by nNano, or an NVIDIA


--- Page 3 ---
Fig. 1: System model architecture and split-inference pipeline across local on-vehicle platforms (nlocal ∈{nNano, nNX}) and
the AGX Orin aggregator (nAGX). The optimization coordinator executes on the aggregator node, taking telemetry feedback
and channel conditions to issue optimal partition points (zl,k), precision allocations (yl,b), and node assignments (xl,n,k).
Jetson Orin NX (16 GB), denoted by nNX. The edge aggre-
gator is an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin (32 GB), denoted by
nAGX. For each evaluated local-node configuration, nlocal ∈
{nNano, nNX} and the active compute-node set is
N = {nlocal, nAGX}.
(1)
As illustrated on the left side of Fig. 1, the local node
processes K concurrent inference streams indexed by K =
{1, . . . , K}. Each stream executes an L-layer Vision Trans-
former backbone indexed by L = {1, . . . , L}. For stream
k, layers up to and including the selected cut layer execute
on nlocal. The corresponding intermediate activation tensor is
then transferred over the emulated V2V wireless link, after
which the remaining layers and the 3D detection heads execute
on the edge aggregator nAGX. A layer-specific precision
b ∈B = {8, 16}, corresponding to INT8 and FP16 execution,
is selected for each transformer layer and is shared across
all concurrent streams. The activation tensor size after layer l
under precision b is denoted by S(l, b) in bytes. The available
V2V data rate for stream k is denoted by Rk and varies across
the evaluated link configurations.
B. Decision Variables and Linearization
The optimization couples three decisions that are other-
wise handled independently in conventional split-inference
pipelines: where a stream is partitioned, which node exe-
cutes each layer, and which numerical precision is used for
that layer. These decisions are related because changing the
bitwidth affects both the execution cost of a transformer block
and the size of the activation transmitted across the V2V link
(Fig. 1). For stream k, the binary variable xl,n,k specifies
the node assigned to layer l, while yl,b selects the numerical
precision of that layer. The variable zl,k identifies whether the
execution path is partitioned after layer l:
xl,n,k ∈{0, 1},
(2)
yl,b ∈{0, 1},
(3)
zl,k ∈{0, 1}.
(4)
The precision decision is shared across concurrent streams
because all streams execute the same deployed model configu-
ration, whereas the partition location may differ across streams
according to their link rate and processing condition.
The activation volume after layer l depends on the selected
precision. For a layer with candidate activation sizes S(l, b),
the transmitted volume is written as
Sl(yl) =
X
b∈B
S(l, b)yl,b.
(5)
This term links quantization directly to the communication
cost: selecting INT8 reduces the activation payload relative
to FP16, but may increase the task-quality penalty associated
with that layer.
The computation term depends jointly on placement and
precision, while the communication term depends jointly on
precision and partition location. These products would make
the formulation nonlinear. We therefore introduce the auxiliary
binary variables
wl,n,b,k = xl,n,kyl,b,
(6)
vl,b,k = yl,bzl,k,
(7)
and enforce them exactly using the standard binary lineariza-
tion constraints:
wl,n,b,k ≤xl,n,k,
wl,n,b,k ≤yl,b,
wl,n,b,k ≥xl,n,k + yl,b −1,
(8)
vl,b,k ≤yl,b,
vl,b,k ≤zl,k,
vl,b,k ≥yl,b + zl,k −1.
(9)
Since all participating variables are binary, these constraints
preserve the original products exactly and retain a solvable
MILP formulation.
C. Energy and Latency Models
The cost of a partition depends on both computation and
communication. Executing additional layers locally increases
the work performed by the on-vehicle node but may reduce the
activation size transmitted to the aggregator. Moving the cut


--- Page 4 ---
earlier has the opposite effect. The selected precision further
changes both quantities because INT8 and FP16 have different
execution profiles and activation sizes.
Let τ(l, n, b, K) denote the profiled execution latency of
layer l on node n under precision b with K concurrent streams.
The dependency on K captures the change in layer execution
time under the evaluated multi-stream load. Let Pcomp(n, b)
denote the corresponding profiled active compute power. The
compute energy accumulated across all streams is
Ecomp =

The variable wl,n,b,k ensures that an energy term contributes
only when layer l is assigned to node n and executed at
precision b.
Communication cost is incurred only at the selected par-
tition boundary. If stream k is divided after layer l, the
transmission time is determined by the activation size at that
layer and the available V2V data rate Rk:

The formulation therefore favors later cuts when local exe-
cution is energy-efficient and link conditions are poor, while
earlier cuts become feasible when aggregator execution com-
pensates for the additional transmission cost. The end-to-end
latency of stream k contains all layer execution time on the
selected nodes and the single V2V transfer:

This definition is used directly by the latency constraint and
preserves the measured dependence of computation time on
stream concurrency.
D. MILP Formulation
The optimization selects the partition and precision con-
figuration that minimizes the combined compute and V2V
communication energy:
min
x,y,z,w,v Etotal = Ecomp + Ecomm.
(14)
The objective does not minimize latency directly. Instead,
latency is treated as a feasibility requirement so that an energy-
efficient solution is accepted only when it satisfies the per-
stream completion deadline.
Each layer of every stream must execute on exactly one
active compute node:
X
n∈N
xl,n,k = 1,
∀l ∈L, ∀k ∈K.
(15)
Similarly, each transformer layer is assigned one numerical
precision:
X
b∈B
yl,b = 1,
∀l ∈L.
(16)
Because the precision variables are not stream-indexed, the
resulting layer-wise quantization configuration is common to
all concurrent streams.
The execution path is restricted to one contiguous local-
to-aggregator partition. Once execution moves from nlocal to
nAGX, subsequent layers cannot return to the local node:
xl+1,nlocal,k ≤xl,nlocal,k,
∀l ∈{1, . . . , L −1}, ∀k ∈K.
(17)
The corresponding partition indicator is
zl,k = xl,nlocal,k−xl+1,nlocal,k,
∀l ∈{1, . . . , L−1}, ∀k ∈K.
(18)
To exclude degenerate all-local or all-aggregator assignments,
the first layer is constrained to the local node and the final
layer to the aggregator:
x1,nlocal,k = 1,
∀k ∈K,
(19)
xL,nAGX,k = 1,
∀k ∈K.
(20)
Together, these constraints produce exactly one transition
between the two nodes:
L−1
X
l=1
zl,k = 1,
∀k ∈K.
(21)
The selected configuration must also satisfy the application
latency requirement:
Te2e(k) ≤Tbudget,
∀k ∈K.
(22)
This prevents the optimizer from selecting a low-energy par-
tition that violates the completion deadline under a given
stream load or link rate. Quantization is constrained separately
through an empirically calibrated task-quality budget:
X
l∈L
X
b∈B
∆Q(l, b)yl,b ≤ϵquality.
(23)
Here, ∆Q(l, b) represents the measured sensitivity associated
with quantizing layer l to precision b. This quantity is used
only as the optimization surrogate; final 3D detection accu-
racy is measured using mAP50 on the evaluation workload.
Together with the linearization constraints in (8)–(9), the above
conditions define the feasible set of the MILP.
E. Solver Implementation
As outlined in the coordinator block of Fig. 1, the for-
mulation is implemented in Pyomo 6.7 and solved using
SCIP 8.0 on the Jetson AGX Orin coordinator. For L = 12,
|N| = 2, |B| = 2, and K = 8, the formulation contains
864 binary decision and auxiliary variables. Solver execution
time and solution status are recorded for each evaluated stream
configuration and reported with the experimental results.

IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
To evaluate the proposed optimization framework on em-
bedded vehicular hardware, we deploy a physical testbed
comprising three NVIDIA Jetson Orin platforms under em-
ulated Vehicle-to-Vehicle network traces. This section details
the hardware and software configuration, workload profiling
methodology, V2V link parameterization, and the baseline
deployment strategies used for comparative evaluation.
A. Hardware Testbed and Software Environment
The testbed comprises NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (8 GB)
and Jetson Orin NX (16 GB) platforms as alternative local
compute nodes, nlocal, and a Jetson AGX Orin (32 GB)
as the edge aggregator, nAGX. The platforms are connected
through an emulated vehicular communication link; hardware
specifications are summarized in Table III. All platforms
run NVIDIA JetPack 6.2. Model partitions and INT8/FP16
configurations are executed using TensorRT engines. Active
compute-rail power is sampled at 100 Hz using the onboard
TABLE III: Hardware Testbed and Profiled System Parameters
Parameter

INA3221

INA3221
Texas Instruments INA3221 current and voltage monitors
through the Linux sysfs interfaces. The communication-energy
model uses a wireless interface transmission power of Ptx =
1.8 W.
B. Workload Profiling and Dataset Traces
Evaluation workloads are derived from multi-agent LiDAR
and camera perception traces in the OPV2V benchmark,
including CARLA and Culver City scenarios. The computa-
tional workload uses a 12-layer Vision Transformer backbone
(L = 12, hidden dimension D = 768, 12 attention heads).


--- Page 6 ---
Layer execution latency τ(l, n, b, K) and active compute-
power profiles Pcomp(n, b) are measured separately on the
Orin Nano, Orin NX, and AGX Orin for precision b ∈{8, 16}
and concurrency levels K ∈{2, 4, 6, 8}. Measurements are
collected over 200 inference runs after warm-up. Activation
tensor sizes S(l, b) range from 150 kB to 2.4 MB depending
on layer position and bitwidth. The sensitivity values ∆Q(l, b)
are obtained from layer-wise quantization evaluation on an
independent calibration subset.
C. Network Configuration
For each experiment, the active local node and the AGX
Orin aggregator are connected through an emulated V2V
link. The available data rate for stream k is selected from
{6, 12, 18, 24, 27} Mbps according to the evaluated link con-
figuration. The stream-specific value Rk is used to calculate
intermediate-tensor transmission latency and V2V communi-
cation energy.
D. Baseline Deployment Strategies
The proposed framework is evaluated for both the Orin
Nano–AGX Orin and Orin NX–AGX Orin configurations
under K ∈{2, 4, 6, 8}. Four baseline deployment strategies
are used:
1) Full Local FP16: All L layers execute on nlocal under
FP16 precision.
2) Static Early Split (l = 3, FP16): Layers 1–3 execute on
nlocal, while layers 4–12 execute on nAGX under FP16
precision.
3) Static Late Split (l = 8, FP16): Layers 1–8 execute on
nlocal, while layers 9–12 execute on nAGX under FP16
precision.
4) Uniform INT8 Split (l = 4): Execution is divided after
layer 4, with all layers quantized uniformly to INT8.
Task quality is measured using 3D bounding-box detec-
tion mAP50. System-level metrics include end-to-end task
completion latency Te2e, compute energy Ecomp, and V2V
communication energy Ecomm.
V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
This section evaluates the proposed optimization frame-
work against four baseline deployment strategies for K ∈
{2, 4, 6, 8}. Experiments cover both local-to-aggregator con-
figurations: Jetson Orin Nano paired with Jetson AGX Orin
and Jetson Orin NX paired with Jetson AGX Orin.
A. Energy Consumption and Multi-Stream Allocation
Table II reports compute energy on the local node and
aggregator, modeled V2V communication energy, total energy,
average end-to-end task completion latency, and 3D detection
mAP50. Energy values are accumulated across the K con-
current streams, whereas Te2e reports the average completion
latency per stream. Static FP16 splits transmit the intermediate
activation at the selected partition without reducing its numeri-
cal precision. For the Orin Nano configuration, the Early Split
(l = 3) produces a 1.8 MB activation and requires 0.38 J
of communication energy at K = 2, increasing to 1.54 J at
K = 8. The Late Split (l = 8) produces a 2.4 MB activation,
resulting in 0.46 J and 1.84 J at the same stream counts.
The proposed formulation jointly selects the partition loca-
tion and layer precision. Layers whose calibrated INT8 penal-
ties satisfy constraint (23) can execute at reduced precision,
while the stream-specific cut determines the activation trans-
mitted over the V2V link. Communication energy increases
from 0.14 J at K = 2 to 0.55 J at K = 8. Relative to
the Uniform INT8 split, this corresponds to a 33.3–36.0%
reduction across the evaluated stream counts. Relative to the
FP16 static splits, the reduction ranges from 63.2% to 70.1%
for the reported comparisons. Total energy combines compute
energy on both active nodes and modeled V2V transmission
energy. On the Orin Nano configuration, Full Local FP16
increases from 0.88 J at K = 2 to 3.92 J at K = 8 as
concurrent load increases. At K = 8, the proposed method
requires 3.07 J, corresponding to a 21.7% reduction relative
to Full Local FP16. The reduction relative to Uniform INT8
is smaller, from 3.16 J to 3.07 J (2.8%), while the proposed
configuration also provides lower latency and higher mAP50.
B. End-to-End Latency and Stream Scaling
End-to-end latency increases with concurrency because the
profiled layer latency τ(l, n, b, K) includes the effect of si-
multaneous inference streams on each compute node. On
the Orin Nano, Full Local FP16 increases from 58.4 ms at
K = 2 to 248.5 ms at K = 8. Static partitioning reduces the
computation assigned to the local node but introduces V2V
transfer delay, whose contribution depends on the activation
size at the selected cut and the available stream-specific link
rate. At K = 8, the proposed method reaches 98.4 ms on the
Orin Nano, compared with 149.2 ms for Uniform INT8 and
176.2 ms for the Static Early Split. These values correspond
to latency reductions of 34.0% and 44.2%, respectively. On
the Orin NX, the proposed configuration reaches 86.7 ms,
compared with 129.5 ms for Uniform INT8 and 158.6 ms for
the Static Early Split, giving reductions of 33.1% and 45.3%.
C. 3D Detection Accuracy and Precision Allocation
Unified FP16 execution provides a reference 3D detection
accuracy of 79.2% mAP50. Uniform INT8 execution reaches
74.3% at K = 8, corresponding to a 4.9 percentage-point re-
duction. The layer-wise sensitivity calibration shows that quan-
tization sensitivity is non-monotonic across the transformer
backbone. As shown in Fig. 2(a), layers l ∈{1, 6, 9, 11, 12}
incur comparatively larger INT8 sensitivity penalties and are
retained in FP16, whereas layers l ∈{2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10} have
lower penalties and are assigned INT8. The resulting allocation
satisfies the quality constraint in (23) while avoiding uniform
quantization across layers with different measured sensitivities.
The communication effect of the selected precision con-
figuration is shown in Fig. 2(b). At layers l ∈{2, 3, 4, 5},
the intermediate activation size decreases from 1.8 MB under
FP16 to 0.9 MB under INT8. The optimizer selects partition
points within l ∈{3, 4, 5} for the bandwidth-constrained


--- Page 7 ---
(a) Layer-wise INT8 sensitivity and selected FP16/INT8 assignment.
(b) Intermediate activation size across candidate partition layers.
Fig. 2: Effect of layer-wise mixed-precision selection on quantization sensitivity and intermediate activation size.
cases, thereby combining a smaller transmitted activation with
reduced-precision execution before the V2V transfer. Layers
retained in FP16 preserve the corresponding FP16 activa-
tion representation. Across all evaluated stream counts, the
proposed mixed-precision configuration achieves 75.1–76.1%
mAP50 on the Orin Nano and 75.3–76.1% on the Orin NX.
Relative to the 79.2% FP16 reference, the measured reduction
remains within 3.1–4.1 percentage points.
D. Solver Execution Runtime
The SCIP 8.0 solver runs on the AGX Orin coordinator.
SCIP returns an optimal solution for each evaluated instance
without reaching the configured time limit. Solver time in-
creases with stream count, from 4.2 ms to 8.4 ms on the Orin
Nano configuration and from 4.1 ms to 8.1 ms on the Orin NX
configuration as K increases from 2 to 8. Across all evaluated
stream counts, solver execution remains below 10 ms.
VI. CONCLUSION
This paper explored an edge orchestration framework for
split inference of vision transformer in connected automated
vehicles. The framework jointly optimizes adaptive model
partitioning and layer-wise INT8/FP16 selection through a
Mixed-Integer Linear Program that minimizes compute and
communication energy subject to end-to-end latency and task-
quality constraints. The framework was evaluated on Jetson
Orin Nano, Jetson Orin NX, and Jetson AGX Orin plat-
forms using OPV2V-driven multi-stream workloads with K ∈
2, 4, 6, 8. Across the evaluated configurations, joint partition
and precision selection reduces V2V communication energy
by 33.3–36.0% relative to the Uniform INT8 split and by
up to 70.1% relative to the static FP16 splits. At K = 8,
end-to-end latency decreases from 149.2 ms to 98.4 ms on
the Orin Nano and from 129.5 ms to 86.7 ms on the Orin
NX relative to Uniform INT8. The selected mixed-precision
configurations limit the reduction in 3D detection accuracy
to 3.1–4.1 percentage points in mAP50 relative to FP16
execution. Future exploration will consider communication-
aware intermediate token reduction and targeting additional
V2X link conditions.
